manifesto.loud: We sell the silence that comes

lab.title: The Lab
body: Most banyas abroad replicate a fixed template — the same parilka, the same temperature, the same protocol, every time. We respect the tradition, and we do not stop there.

In a country the size of Russia the ritual split into hundreds of local variations — Siberian, Altai, Karelian, Ural, village traditions that never reached a textbook. Our masters come from that living tradition and keep working inside it. We read old practitioner notes. We travel back to masters who carry local knowledge. We test, we keep what works, we discard what does not.

It also means no two masters here work the same way. Max builds hard contrast and drives it through you. Yura reads your breath and skin and balances the steam on the edge of what your body will take. Same ritual, different hands, and you will feel which one you are under.
That is what Lab means. Same ancient foundation. Active experimentation on top of it. Every session is, in some small way, an experiment — and you are in the room for it.

comparison.title: Banya is not a sauna
comparison.note: Most Americans picture the cedar box at the gym. That runs at 150–175°F and often bans water on the stones outright. Here is the actual difference.

vocabulary.meaning: The ritual itself. Never sauna, never steam room, never bathhouse.
The act of working the body with steam and venik. The verb and the craft.
A bundle of fresh oak or birch branches, used by the master.
Never attendant, never therapist. The master leads the ritual.
The state afterwards. What people come back for.

answers.question: Is a banya the same as a sauna?
answers.short: No. A sauna is Finnish, dry and silent — you sit in it. A banya is Russian, wet and alive — you are worked on.
body: A Finnish sauna runs 175–200°F at low humidity, and you sit in it alone. A Russian banya runs 180–210°F at 50–60% humidity, and a master moves the steam across your body with a bundle of fresh oak branches called a venik.

The American gym sauna is a third thing again: 150–175°F, almost no humidity, and water on the stones is often banned outright for liability reasons. Most people in Hawaii have never experienced either real tradition.
The practical difference is that a banya is done to you, in rounds, over about two hours, with cold water between them. A sauna is something you sit in for fifteen minutes.

answers.question: Where does banya come from?
answers.short: From the Slavic village bathhouse — for most of its history the cleanest and hottest room a family had, and the one they used for everything that mattered.
body: Written accounts of bathhouses in Slavic lands run back to the medieval chronicles, and the practice is older than the writing about it. For centuries a banya was a small log building at the edge of a household, heated by a stove packed with stones.

The oldest form is the black banya, built without a chimney. The fire burns, smoke fills the room and blackens the walls, and when the wood is spent the smoke is let out while the heat stays in the stone. Chimneys came later. Practitioners still argue about which gives better air.

It was never only about washing. In village life the banya was the cleanest heated space a family had, so it was where women gave birth, where the sick were brought, and where the dead were prepared. A thousand years of a culture's most serious moments happened in that room. That is the weight the word carries, and it is why we do not call this a spa.

The venik came out of the same practicality. Birch and oak grow everywhere in those forests. The branches are cut in early summer while the leaf is still soft, dried through the year, and soaked back to life in hot water before a session.

answers.question: Why beat someone with oak branches?
answers.short: It is not beating. The venik moves hot air onto the skin, and the master uses it to put heat exactly where he wants it, in the amount your body will take.
body: The air directly against your skin sits still and insulates you. That layer is the reason a person can be in a room at 200°F at all. The venik breaks it. Every sweep pushes hot, wet air onto the body, and heat that was hanging in the room goes into you instead.

That is the whole mechanism, and it is why the venik is a tool rather than a ritual prop. Held high, it takes heat from the ceiling, where the hottest air collects. Pressed flat against the back, it holds that heat against the skin. Lifted and fanned, it cools. A master spends the round deciding where the heat goes and how fast.

The leaves matter for ordinary reasons. Oak is thick and stiff, carries hot steam well and survives several sessions. Birch is softer and more aromatic, and easier on skin that has not done this before. Both are cut fresh in early summer and soaked before use — a dry venik crumbles and scratches.

The percussion is real, and light. It brings blood to the skin and gives the body a steady stream of sensation to attend to. That is a large part of why a round feels like something being done to you rather than something you are getting through.

answers.question: What do the heat and the cold actually do?
answers.short: Heat raises core temperature and loads the heart and circulation the way moderate exercise does. Cold reverses it within seconds. Here is what is known about that, and what is not.
body: In the heat, blood moves to the skin, heart rate climbs into a range comparable with moderate exercise, and you sweat heavily. Do it often enough and the body adapts to heat the way it adapts to a training load.

In cold water the opposite happens almost instantly. Vessels close, breathing catches, and the body releases a large amount of noradrenaline. That is the source of the clean, wide-awake state people describe afterwards, and it is why the cold is not a flourish at the end of the session but half of the mechanism.

Most of the research that exists is Finnish and concerns their dry sauna. The largest long-running study followed 1,688 Finnish adults for a median of fifteen years and found that people bathing four to seven times a week had markedly lower cardiovascular mortality than those going once a week — a hazard ratio of 0.23 after adjustment for risk factors. That number is worth reading carefully. It is observational, not a trial: people who sit in a sauna five times a week may differ from those who do not in ways no statistical adjustment catches. The authors state plainly that results from Finnish sauna cannot be transferred directly to other kinds of steam room.

So the honest position is this. Heat and cold do real and measurable things to the body, and people have organised their week around them for a thousand years for reasons that were never mystical. What we will not tell you is that two hours on a boat will fix anything in particular. Come for what the ritual does in the room and in the hours after it, and hold everything beyond that as an open question.

sources.title: Sauna bathing and cardiovascular mortality — BMC Medicine, 2018

answers.question: Why real fire, and never an electric heater?
answers.short: Because the steam comes off a heavy mass of stone that has been heated for hours, and an electric element cannot hold heat the way a fired stove does.
body: Steam in a banya is not made by a machine. It is made by a ladle of water thrown onto stones. What matters is the mass of that stone and how hot it is: hot enough to flash the water instantly into a fine steam that feels dry on the skin, and heavy enough to do it again a minute later without going cold.

The heaters in most gyms and hotels hold a fraction of that stone and run cooler. Water on them gives a damp, heavy cloud instead of a burst — when it is permitted at all, which in American gyms it often is not, for liability reasons. This is the single biggest reason a gym sauna and a banya are not the same experience, and why people who have only met the former have no useful reference for the latter.

A real fire adds the rest of it: the sound, the smell in the room, and a heat curve that rises and falls instead of sitting on a thermostat setting. Working with that curve rather than against it is part of the craft.

answers.question: Why do athletes use banya?
answers.short: For recovery between hard sessions, for sleep, and for a nervous system that will not come down on its own. With one caveat about timing that most places will not mention.
body: Fighters, watermen and lifters are among the most consistent banya people anywhere, and not for the atmosphere. Heat brings blood to tissue that has been worked, the cold cuts the sensation of soreness sharply, and most people sleep unusually deeply the night after. Across a hard training block that combination is worth a great deal.

The caveat is about timing. If your goal is muscle size, do not go into cold water straight after lifting. Controlled work has found that cold water immersion immediately after resistance training reduces the anabolic signalling and the muscle fibre growth the training was meant to produce. Strength gains held up in that work; size did not. Endurance training does not appear to be affected the same way.

In practice this is a scheduling question, not a reason to stay away. A banya on a rest day, or several hours after training, or after conditioning rather than after heavy lifting. Tell the master what you trained and when — it changes how the session is run.

sources.title: Cold water immersion and resistance training adaptation — Journal of Applied Physiology, 2019
Post-exercise cold water immersion and hypertrophy: meta-analysis — European Journal of Sport Science, 2024

answers.question: Why do you call it Russian?
answers.short: Because it is. The origin is the credential, and softening it into something vaguer would make the thing itself harder to understand.
body: Russian banya carries the same kind of weight in heat ritual that Italian espresso carries in coffee. Naming the origin is not nationalism, it is accuracy — it tells you which tradition the room, the stove, the steam and the venik came from, and therefore what is about to happen to you.
Some people pause at the word. We would rather they paused than arrived expecting a spa. The word is part of how the room stays what it is.

One distinction we make openly: this is cultural, not political. Our masters are Russian and Ukrainian and work side by side over a craft older than any border between them. We talk about the tradition and the people who carry it, never about a state.

answers.question: Why is it silent, and why do you take phones?
answers.short: Because nothing works while someone in the room might be performing, and a phone in the room means someone might be.
body: Phones are collected at boarding. It is required rather than suggested, and it is the rule people thank us for afterwards.

There are two practical reasons. A guest who could be photographed does not let go, and letting go is the entire session. And everyone else in the room needs to know that it cannot happen — the trust in that room is the product.

Silence works the same way. During par nobody speaks, because the master is reading your breathing and conversation is noise in that signal. Between rounds the quiet is what lets the heat settle. Talking starts again over tea at the end, if it starts at all. Most people find they would rather it did not.

answers.question: What actually happens in a session?
answers.short: Four rounds of heat, venik and cold water over about two hours, led by a master, in silence.
body: You arrive, hand over your phone, drink tea and stop talking. The first round is gentle — the body needs to adapt before anything is done to it.

In the second round the master works you with the venik: steam is pushed along the body, held, released. This is par, and it is the centre of the ritual. Then cold — a plunge, or cold water poured over you — and then rest on deck, in silence.
That cycle repeats three to four times. It ends with tea and no conversation. Most people are quiet for an hour afterwards. That part is called the afterglow, and it is what people come back for.

answers.question: How hot is it, and is it safe?
answers.short: The air holds 180–210°F, but you are never left alone in it, and every round ends before it needs to.
body: The heat is real and the humidity is high, which makes it feel far stronger than a dry sauna at the same temperature. That is the point — the contrast between hot and cold is the mechanism.

You are not in there by yourself. The master reads breath, skin and posture through the whole round and adjusts the steam and the pressure of the venik to what your body is actually taking. Rounds are short. You leave the heat before you want to, not after.

Heat and cold contrast puts load on the heart. If you are pregnant, have a heart condition or blood pressure that is being managed, or you are on medication that affects how you handle heat, ask your doctor first and tell the master before the session. We would rather have that conversation at the dock than in the parilka.

answers.question: What do I bring, and what happens to my phone?
answers.short: Swimwear, a towel and nothing else. Phones are collected at boarding and returned at the end.
body: Bring swimwear and a towel. Slippers if you like. Everything used in the ritual — veniks, tea, cold water — is ours.
Phones are surrendered at boarding. This is required, not suggested. The reset does not happen while a device is in the room, and no one relaxes while someone else might be filming.
Eat lightly beforehand and drink water through the day. No alcohol before or during the ritual.

answers.question: How do I book, and how do I pay?
answers.short: Send an application through this site. A master replies, confirms a date with you, and sends a payment link from the business — card, receipt, no cash in an envelope.
body: There is no open calendar on this site, on purpose. Sessions are small, the masters are few, and the ocean has an opinion about the schedule. So you send an application with roughly when suits you and how many of you there are, and a master comes back to you with a time.

Once the time is agreed you get a payment link. It is a card payment to the business, it produces a real receipt, and you can pay for yourself and for the people you are bringing in one go. Nothing is charged before a human has confirmed your date.
If you want to give a session to someone else, say so in the application and we will send the same link with a note instead of a date.
